annotations.keyFindings: Station pass rates were 88 percent after near-peer teaching and 86 percent after faculty teaching; mean station score difference 0.9 points (95 percent CI -1.8 to 3.6).
annotations.limitations: One school, 124 students; too small to exclude a difference below 10 percentage points; four sessions only.

annotations.keyFindings: 32 studies (7 randomised) mostly found similar or better learner performance with near-peer teaching; only 4 reported costs and none valued tutor time.
annotations.limitations: Heterogeneous outcomes measured soon after teaching; search to 2020.

annotations.keyFindings: Faculty-led teaching cost 46 units per student contact hour and near-peer teaching 11 units, rising to 19 units when tutor time was valued.
annotations.limitations: Costs only; one school; one year.
annotations.notes: Shows how the result depends on valuing tutor time.

annotations.keyFindings: The 5.2-point advantage of optional near-peer attenders shrank to 1.1 points after adjustment for first-year scores and sex.
annotations.limitations: Residual confounding; three years at one school.

annotations.keyFindings: 18 tutors described consolidating knowledge and feedback skills but also time pressure before finals and uncertainty about correcting technique.
Near-peer tutors left 22 percent of technique errors uncorrected versus 12 percent for faculty, falling to 15 percent after a one-hour calibration session.
annotations.limitations: 60 sessions at one school; tutors knew they were recorded.

claims.text: In a randomised comparison of 124 second-year students, station pass rates were 88 percent after near-peer teaching and 86 percent after faculty teaching.
claims.passage: Station pass rates were 88 percent after near-peer teaching and 86 percent after faculty teaching
claims.interpretation: Supports a non-inferiority framing for the effect measure; the study cannot exclude small differences.

claims.text: Faculty-led teaching cost 46 currency units per student contact hour and near-peer teaching 11 units, rising to 19 units when student tutor time was valued.
claims.passage: When the time of student tutors was valued at the rate paid for research assistant work, the near-peer cost rose to 19 units.
claims.interpretation: Tutor time must be valued explicitly and tested in a sensitivity analysis.

claims.text: When attendance was optional, the 5.2-point score advantage of near-peer attenders shrank to 1.1 points after adjustment for first-year scores.
claims.passage: The unadjusted difference in OSCE examination-station scores between attenders and non-attenders was 5.2 points, which shrank to 1.1 points after adjustment for first-year scores and sex.
claims.interpretation: Existing attendance data cannot give a fair effect estimate; allocation by timetable is needed.

claims.text: Near-peer tutors left 22 percent of technique errors uncorrected compared with 12 percent for faculty tutors, and 15 percent after a one-hour calibration session.
claims.passage: Near-peer tutors left 22 percent of technique errors uncorrected compared with 12 percent for faculty tutors.
claims.interpretation: Calibration training belongs in the cost of the near-peer option.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One small randomised comparison and a review of 32 studies suggest that near-peer teaching of examination skills gives similar results to faculty teaching, but they cannot exclude small differences. A single-school costing shows near-peer teaching is much cheaper per contact hour, less so when tutor time is valued. Comparisons based on optional attendance are dominated by self-selection. Near-peer tutors miss more technique errors, which a short calibration session reduces. The evidence supports an economic evaluation with a fair comparison of groups and explicit valuation of tutor time.
gradeRationale: One small randomised study and a heterogeneous review for effect, single-school observational costing, and confounded attendance data; direction consistent but imprecise and indirect.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
